parole.significato: wall walk, allure (protected pathway on a wall of a city or castle)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic الدَّرْب (ad-dárb), from Arabic دَرْب (darb, “path, pass, way”).

parole.significato: customs (agency that collect the taxes on imported goods)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aduana, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic *الدوان (ad-duwān, “the administrative office”), from Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān), borrowed from Classical Persian دیوَان (dēwān), from Middle Persian d(p)ywʾn' (dēwān, “archive, collected writings”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic دُفَّة, from Arabic دَفَّة (daffa).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic عَرْض (ʕarḍ). Compare Spanish alarde.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic القواد (al-qawwád), from Arabic قَوَّاد (qawwād). Cognate with Spanish alcahuete.

parole.significato: alcaide (commander of a province or fortress)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alcaide, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الْقَائِد (al-qāʔid, “the leader”).
From Andalusian Arabic اَلْأَرْز (al-ʔarz), from Classical Arabic أَرْز (ʔarz, “cedar”).

parole.significato: cutlass (European sword with a straight or slightly curved blade)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic خَنْجَر (ḵanjar).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic اَلْغَار (al-ḡár), from Arabic اَلْغَار (al-ḡār, “grotto”).
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic القُطُن (al-quṭun), variant of Arabic قُطْن (quṭn); see cotton for more. Doublet of cotão.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aljuba, from Andalusian Arabic الجبة (al-gubba), from Arabic الْجُبَّة (al-jubba). Doublet of gibão. Cognate with Spanish aljuba.

parole.significato: almagra (a deep red ochre found in Spain)
parole.testo: From earlier almagra, from Andalusian Arabic المغرة (almáḡra), from Arabic الْمَغْرَة (al-maḡra), الْمُغْرَة (al-muḡra, “red clay or earth”).

parole.significato: almanac (book or table listing astronomical, nautical or other events for the year)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic اَلْمَنَاخ (al-manāḵ, “climate”), from Byzantine Greek ἀλμενιχιακά (almenikhiaká, “calendar”), probably ultimately of Coptic origin. See almanac for more.
Borrowed from Arabic المِخَدَّة (al-miḵadda, “the pillow/cushion”), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Spanish almohada.
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic المِهْرَاس (al-mihrās).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese almogavar, from Andalusian Arabic المُغَاوِر (al-muḡā́wir), from Arabic مُغَاوِر (muḡāwir).

parole.significato: muezzin (person who issues call to prayer)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic اَلْمُؤَذِّن (al-muʔaḏḏin, “the muezzin”). Doublet of muezim.

parole.significato: almude, a traditional unit of liquid volume equal to 14–26 liters depending on the area of Portugal
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic المُدّ (al-mudd), from Arabic مُدّ (mudd), probably via Aramaic 𐡬𐡣𐡩𐡠 (mdyʾ) and מוֹדְיָא (moḏyā) or Classical Syriac ܡܘܿܕܝܳܐ (moḏyā) from Akkadian 𒉘𒈨𒌍 (/⁠maddattu/middattu⁠/, “kind of vessel, unit of volume”). Cognate with Ancient Greek μόδιος (módios), Latin modius, and Spani

From Andalusian Arabic البُنْدُقَة (al-bunduqa), from Arabic بُنْدُق (bunduq, “hazelnut, pebble, bullet, gun”), from Middle Persian pndk' (pondik, “hazelnut”), from Ancient Greek Ποντικὸν κάρυον (Pontikòn káruon, “Pontic nut”). Compare Spanish albóndiga.

parole.significato: agitation; turmoil; bustle; ruckus (frenetic, chaotic activity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alvoroço, from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic البُرُوز (al-burūz).

parole.significato: reward given to someone bringing good news or something that was lost
parole.testo: From alvíssara, from Old Galician-Portuguese alvyssara, from Andalusian Arabic البِشَرَة (al-bišara), from Arabic بُشْرَى (bušrā). Cognate with Galician albízaras, Spanish albricias and Mozarabic albixara.
Borrowed from Arabic نِيل (nīl) via Andalusian Arabic, from Persian نیل (nil, “indigo”), from Middle Persian, ultimately from Sanskrit नील (nīla, “dark blue”).

parole.significato: arroba, a traditional unit of mass, equivalent to 14.7 kg
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese arroba and arrova, from Andalusian Arabic and Arabic اَلرُّبْع (ar-rubʕ, “fourth”) in reference to its making up one-fourth of a quintal. Cognate with Galician and Spanish arroba, Catalan arrova, and Maltese raba’.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arroz, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic روز (rawz), from Arabic *رَوْز (*rawz), from رُزّ (ruzz), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza), from Proto-Iranian *wrinǰiš, from *wriHǰíš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *wriHǰʰíš.

parole.significato: watermill with a vertical water wheel
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atafona, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic طَاحُونَة (ṭāḥūna). Compare Galician tafona and Spanish tahona.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azeite, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic زَيْت (zayt). Compare Galician and Spanish aceite.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azaveche, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic سبج (sabáj), from Arabic سَبَج (sabaj), borrowed from Middle Persian špk' (/⁠šabag⁠/), from šp (/⁠šab⁠/), from Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐎱 (x-š-p /⁠xšapa⁠/), from Proto-Iranian *xšáfš, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšáps, from Proto-Ind
From Andalusian Arabic الزَّوْق (az-zawq, “the quicksilver”), from Arabic زَاؤُوق (zāʔūq, “quicksilver”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese açafram, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الزَّعْفَرَان (az-zaʕfarān), from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān). Cognate with Asturian, Galician, and Spanish azafrán.
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic سَوْسَن (sawsan), borrowed from Middle Persian, from Ancient Greek σοῦσον (soûson), borrowed from Egyptian zšn. Cognate with Galician and Spanish azucena.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese açúcar, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic السُكَّر (as-sukkar), from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *
From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic كَهْرَبَاء (kahrabāʔ).

parole.significato: celamim, a traditional unit of dry volume equivalent to 0.4–0.6 litres in different 19th-century contexts
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese ceramin, from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic ثُمُنِ (ṯumuni, “of one-eighth”). Cognate with Galician celamín and Spanish celemín.

parole.significato: migraine (kind of headache, usually affecting only one side of the head)
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic الشَقِيقَة (aš-šaqīqa). Compare Galician and Old Spanish xaqueca, Spanish jaqueca.

parole.significato: fanga, Portuguese sack, a traditional unit of dry volume equal to about 50–75 litres at different places and times
parole.testo: From Andalusian Arabic فَنِيقَة (faníqa, “sack”), from Arabic فَنِيقَة (fanīqa). Cognate with Spanish fanega.

Possibly from garfa (“animal's claw”), from Andalusian Arabic جَارْفَا (gārfā, “handful”), from Arabic غُرْفَة (ḡurfa, “cup or dipper”), from غَرَفَ (ḡarafa, “to ladle”), with influence from garfio (“hook”). Or, possibly from Vulgar Latin *garra, from Gaulish *garrā (“leg”) (compare Breton gar, Old
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese louco, possibly from Andalusian Arabic لَوَق (lawaq, “stupidity”), from Arabic لاق (lāq, “to soften”). Compare Galician louco, Spanish loco and Sicilian loccu.
From Andalusian Arabic مَكِيلَة (makíla), from Arabic مَكِيلَة (makīla, “measured”). Cognate with Spanish maquila.

parole.significato: reef (rocks at or near surface of the water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic, from Arabic رَصِيف (raṣīf).
From Andalusian Arabic رَكْبَة (rakba), from Arabic رَكَبَة (rakaba), plural of رَاكِب (rākib, “rider”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese xedrez, borrowed from Andalusian Arabic الشَطْرَنْج (aš-šaṭranj), from Arabic شَطْرَنْج (šaṭranj), borrowed from Classical Persian چَتْرَنگ (čatrang), from Middle Persian 𐭰𐭠𐭲𐭫𐭠𐭭𐭢 (cʾtlʾng /⁠čatrang⁠/, “chess”), borrowed from Sanskrit चतुरङ्ग (caturaṅga, “compri
Borrowed from Andalusian Arabic زَغَال (zaḡāl, “young; brave”), from Arabic زَغْلُول (zaḡlūl, “boy”).
